extracted.intended_audience: transfusion_service_laboratory_staff; blood bank directors; clinical laboratory scientists; public health professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Selecting and evaluating laboratory techniques for routine screening of blood donations for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), balancing sensitivity, specificity, throughput, cost, and operational practicality. The page reports comparative performance of C.I.E.P., R.P.H.A., and R.I.A. and gives recommendations for routine replacement of less effective methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection rate / sensitivity for HBsAg
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative detection counts: on screening of 22,239 donations C.I.E.P. detected 27 sera positive for HBsAg, R.P.H.A. 39, and R.I.A. 41; R.I.A. increased the detection rate by more than half over C.I.E.P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer methods with higher detection rates to identify more infected donations; R.I.A. and R.P.H.A. detected substantially more positives than C.I.E.P. in the study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize false negatives (safety consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: False negatives by screening led to transfusion-transmitted HBsAg-positive hepatitis: ten donors initially negative on first screening were HBsAg positive at the next donation; retesting found nine had been positive at the earlier donation, and further false-negative donations by C.I.E.P. caused six cases of HBsAg-positive hepatitis (one fatal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screening methods must minimize false negatives because missed infections can result in transfusion-transmitted hepatitis and serious outcomes; selection should prioritize sensitivity where public-health impact is high.

rubrics_metrics.name: False positive rate / specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of false positive reactions when using R.P.H.A. or R.I.A. for screening was less than 1%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable specificity is important to avoid unnecessary donor deferral and confirmatory workload; R.P.H.A. and R.I.A. demonstrated low false-positive rates in this evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Throughput / daily testing capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational throughput demonstrated: as many as 700 donations in one day have been tested by R.P.H.A. or R.I.A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods chosen for routine screening must support the volume of donations processed by a service; demonstrated high-throughput capability is a practical requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed / turnaround time
rubrics_metrics.description: R.P.H.A. is described as faster than R.I.A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faster assays facilitate timely screening and operational efficiency; speed is a key factor when balancing method selection for routine use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost / expense
rubrics_metrics.description: R.P.H.A. is less expensive than R.I.A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cost considerations (reagent, equipment, personnel) affect feasibility for routine adoption; cheaper methods with acceptable performance may be preferred in resource-constrained settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity / assay subjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: R.I.A. is more objective compared with other methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective assays reduce reader-dependent variability and improve reproducibility; objectivity is desirable for consistent routine screening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for routine screening / practicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusion/recommendation: either R.P.H.A. or R.I.A. should replace C.I.E.P. as the routine method of screening donor sera for HBsAg.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method choice for routine screening should balance improved detection, acceptable specificity, throughput, cost, and objectivity; the paper recommends replacing less effective routine methods with R.P.H.A. or R.I.A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of donor sera for retesting and evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Preservation of all donor sera already tested for HBsAg by C.I.E.P. allowed C.I.E.P., R.P.H.A., and R.I.A. to be evaluated and retested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retaining sera enables retrospective comparison, confirmatory testing, and investigation of false negatives; sample preservation is an important operational quality-control practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for confirmatory / repeat testing to resolve discordant results
rubrics_metrics.description: Retesting with R.P.H.A. and R.I.A. revealed that some donations initially apparently negative were actually positive on earlier tests; confirmatory assays changed case ascertainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement confirmatory or repeat testing protocols to resolve discordant or borderline results and to reduce both false negatives and false positives.
